title: Generation Z: Media Consumption and MIL
screen_reason: Online questionnaire survey of 115 Greek pupils and undergraduates aged 12-24 (published December 2022) on media consumption, social-network use and stances towards disinformation. One item asks how often respondents encounter fake news and reports a share above a threshold: 25.2% answered 'often'. Under the protocol a 'how often' scale qualifies when a share of respondents above a threshold is given, so the paper is eligible - just barely. The study's other misinformation item (58.3% say they have been deceived by news later proven fake) is a belief/deception measure and is excluded.

estimates.country: Greece (respondents from different areas of Northern Greece, especially Thrace and South Macedonia)
estimates.platform: Not platform-specific; online questionnaire about fake news encountered in their media environment
estimates.date: Not stated; article received 11 October 2022 and accepted 19 December 2022, so fieldwork was in or before 2022
estimates.measure_type: % of surveyed 12-24-year-olds who said they encounter fake news 'often'
estimates.value_raw: 25,2% answered often (alongside 28,7% 'not very often' and 22,6% 'rarely'; the reported categories sum to 76.5%, so at least one further response option is not reported)
estimates.denominator: 115 Greek pupils and undergraduate students aged 12-24 (45.2% male, 54.8% female; 31% aged 12-15, 33% 16-19, 36% 20-24)
estimates.definition: Respondent selected 'often' on a frequency scale asking how often they encounter fake news; fake news is respondent-defined, with no examples or external verification
estimates.misinfo_def: No definition of fake news or disinformation is given anywhere in the paper; the questionnaire block is described only as “variables related to disinformation and fake news”.
estimates.source_quote: The percentages regarding the frequency they encounter fake news are the following: 28,7% answered not very often, 25,2% answered often and 22,6% answered rarely (Figure 10).
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 467 (Figure 11: 'Frequency of Fake News Feed Spotted by Gen Zers')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Purely respondent judgment. Nothing is coded or verified by anyone: no examples of fake news are shown, no definition is supplied to respondents, and no reliability or validity statistics are reported for the instrument, which is described only as adapted from an earlier questionnaire.
estimates.moderator_quote: In order to achieve the most representative sample, we posted the questionnaire to nation-wide social media groups asking members of the desired age group to respond anonymously. To reach out to populations of younger ages that may not have a social media account, we asked members to pass the questionnaires to this age group ... based on the snowball effect method. We gathered responses from a total sample of 115 young people students aged between 12 and 24 years old.
estimates.notes: Weak but admissible. The response categories reported (not very often 28.7%, often 25.2%, rarely 22.6%) sum to only 76.5%, so the remaining ~23.5% sit in unreported categories (presumably 'never' and/or 'very often') and no 'any exposure' share can be derived without a barred cross-category computation - hence only the verbatim 'often' share is recorded. The scale labels are also not presented in a consistent order, the underlying figure is not reproduced in the text, and the text mislabels it Figure 10 where the caption says Figure 11. Sample is 115 self-selected respondents recruited by posting a link into Greek social-media groups plus snowballing, so it is a convenience sample, not a representative one, despite the authors' claim of representativeness; ages start at 12.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (a) '58,3% (n=67) responded positively' to 'the question of the participants' being DECEIVED by news that has later proven to be fake' - this is self-reported deception, i.e. belief in false news, which the protocol excludes. The results section glosses it as '58,3% stated that they have been influenced by disinformation', and the discussion frames it as 'their reactions upon identifying it', which could be read as an encounter item; but the explicit wording on p. 470 ('being deceived by news that has later proven to be fake') settles it as belief, so it is dropped rather than coded as exposure. Flagging it because a coder working from the results paragraph alone could plausibly have extracted it as a 58.3% exposure estimate. (b) Reactions on being deceived (67.1% ignored it, 20.7% reported it, 12.2% commented) - post-hoc responses among the deceived subgroup, not exposure or sharing; note that 'commented on it' is not sharing misinformation. (c) Media-use shares (93.9% use smartphones for updates, Instagram/Viber/Facebook/TikTok ownership, 41.7% say their mobile is extremely important, 87% on media effects on education, 73%/72% attitude items) - media use and attitudes, not misinformation. (d) Greece's Media Literacy Index 2021 rank (Cluster 4 of 5, 27th of 35) - an index cited from another source, barred by R8. (e) Figures from Pew, Edelman, We Are Social and the Reuters Digital News Report quoted in the introduction - other studies' numbers.

rob.design: Online self-administered questionnaire, four blocks (sociodemographics, media consumption, social-network consumption, disinformation/fake news), adapted from an earlier instrument (Livingstone and Markha 2007 as cited). Recruitment by posting the link to nation-wide Greek social-media groups and asking members to pass it to younger non-users (snowball); respondents drawn mainly from Northern Greece, Thrace and South Macedonia, partly from schools where the authors had previously run media-literacy programmes. n = 115 aged 12-24; no response rate is computable, no weighting, no power calculation, no reliability or validity statistics, no fieldwork dates. Exposure is a single unanchored frequency item with no definition of fake news given to respondents and with incompletely reported response categories. Reporting is loose throughout (figure numbering, percentages that do not sum).
rob.item6_quote: the team designed an adapted questionnaire in which four different blocks were established: (a) sociodemographic variables, (b) variables related to media consumption, (c) variables related to social network consumption, and (d) variables related to disinformation and fake news.
rob.item10_quote: The percentages regarding the frequency they encounter fake news are the following: 28,7% answered not very often, 25,2% answered often and 22,6% answered rarely.
